name: GitHub Actions
description: GitHub's built-in CI/CD: workflows run on every push, PR and schedule, free for public repos and metered minutes for private ones. The money is in selling pipeline work - migrations, retainer DevOps and fixing deploys that keep breaking.
visits: The default CI/CD for GitHub's 100M+ developer ecosystem; 20,000+ actions in the Marketplace; most open-source projects run on it; Copilot coding agent and Copilot code review now ride on top of it.
pricing_details: Verified from GitHub's official billing docs (October 2026). Plans include monthly Linux minutes: GitHub Free 2,000 min + 500 MB artifact storage; Pro 3,000 min + 1 GB; Team ($4/user/mo) 3,000 min + 2 GB; Enterprise Cloud ($21/user/mo) 50,000 min + 50 GB. Standard hosted runner rates: Linux 2-core $0.006/min, Linux 1-core $0.002/min, Linux arm64 $0.005/min, Windows 2-core $0.010/min (billed at 2x your minute allowance), macOS $0.062/min (billed at 10x). Public repositories: standard runners are completely free, unlimited. Self-hosted runners are always free - you pay only your own server. Overflow storage: $0.25/GB-month shared (artifacts + Packages), $0.07/GB-month cache. Larger runners (16-64 core) cost more per minute and are ALWAYS billed, even on public repos and before your free quota is touched. Storage bills accrue per GB-hour and are not refunded if you delete artifacts mid-cycle. There is an official pricing calculator at github.com/pricing/calculator.
pros: Free and unlimited on public repositories - nothing else in CI comes close for open-source work, and that same free tier is why most portfolios, docs sites and OSS libraries default to it

Zero integration effort if your code already lives on GitHub - workflows sit next to the code, read PR and issue context natively, and there is no webhook dance like Jenkins or a second dashboard like CircleCI
20,000+ ready-made actions in the Marketplace mean the boring 80% (checkout, cache, deploy to Vercel/AWS/Fly, Slack notify) is copy-paste instead of scripting
Self-hosted runners are genuinely free of metered billing, so teams with a spare box or a Kubernetes cluster can bypass per-minute pricing entirely
The AI layer is real, not marketing fluff: Copilot coding agent can pick up failing CI jobs and push a fix PR, and Copilot code review runs as part of the same workflow
cons: The macOS rate is a trap: $0.062/min billed at a 10x multiplier means an iOS or Flutter release build can burn a whole month's free quota in a couple of hours - teams find this out from the invoice, not the docs
Storage billing is sneaky: artifacts and Packages share one quota, usage accrues by the GB-hour, and deleting an artifact today does not refund the bill that already accumulated this cycle

Complex YAML workflows rot fast - deeply nested matrices plus reusable workflows plus environments become a dialect only one person on the team understands, and local debugging (via act or nektos) only approximates the real runner

Locked to the GitHub ecosystem: moving to GitLab or a self-hosted setup means rewriting every workflow; CircleCI and Jenkins configs do not transfer either, but GitHub's gravity makes you forget that until you leave
No meaningful affiliate or reseller program - GitHub's partner route is aimed at cloud resellers and enterprise sales, so the only way to make money from Actions is to sell your own labor around it

faq.question: Is GitHub Actions really free?
faq.answer: For public repositories, yes - standard GitHub-hosted runners are free and unlimited, which is why almost every open-source project uses it. For private repos you get a monthly minute allowance (2,000 on Free, 3,000 on Pro/Team) and metered billing past that. The catch is the multiplier: your allowance is spent at 1x for Linux, 2x for Windows and 10x for macOS, so a private repo doing iOS builds will not stay free for long. Self-hosted runners are the escape hatch - always free of metered billing on any plan.

faq.question: Why did my GitHub Actions bill spike suddenly?
faq.answer: The usual suspects, in order: someone added a macOS job (10x multiplier), a Windows job (2x), a matrix that quietly turned one job into thirty, larger runners (billed even on public repos, quota never applies), or artifact storage creep - artifacts pile up and bill by the GB-hour until retention cleans them. Set spend budgets and the 90%/100% usage alerts in billing settings before you investigate, then check the usage report per workflow file; the offender is usually one recently merged workflow.

faq.question: How does GitHub Actions compare to Jenkins or CircleCI?
faq.answer: Jenkins wins on raw control and plugins but you own a server, its upgrades and its security patches - most small teams should not take that on in 2026. CircleCI still has better caching and a cleaner UX for heavy parallel test suites, and it is cloud-agnostic if you might move off GitHub. Actions wins on ecosystem depth and the fact that it is simply already there. We break the full four-way comparison down in our CI/CD tools article linked below.

faq.question: Can I make money offering GitHub Actions services?
faq.answer: Yes, but as a service provider, not a reseller - there is no affiliate program worth mentioning. The honest plays: one-time pipeline builds and Jenkins migrations ($1,000-5,000 per project), monthly DevOps retainers ($1,000-5,000 per client for maintenance, security patching and on-call fixes), and productized 'your deploy keeps failing' rescue work. Every team with a private repo and a flaky pipeline is a prospect, and the tool being free means your quote is almost pure labor margin.

features: Workflow automation on push, pull request, schedule (cron), manual dispatch and dozens of other triggers, defined as YAML in the repo
Matrix builds - run the same job across OS, runtime and dependency versions in parallel
20,000+ Marketplace actions plus reusable workflows and composite actions for DRY pipelines
Hosted runners on Linux, Windows and macOS (Intel and arm64), plus always-free self-hosted runners
Environments with required reviewers, secrets protection and deploy gates for staging/production discipline
AI layer: Copilot coding agent picks up CI failures and pushes fix PRs; Copilot code review runs on Actions infrastructure
OIDC federation for keyless cloud auth to AWS/GCP/Azure - no long-lived credentials in secrets
Caching for dependencies and Docker layers, artifact storage, and a pricing calculator for cost planning
platform: Web UI and YAML workflows inside github.com; runs on GitHub-hosted Linux/Windows/macOS runners or your own self-hosted machines; mobile visibility through the GitHub apps; CLI via gh workflow/gh run commands.
content:
GitHub Actions has quietly become the default answer to "how does this code get deployed?" - not because it is the most powerful CI system (it is not) or the cheapest at scale (it often is not), but because it lives where the code already lives. If your team is on GitHub, the pipeline conversation is basically over before it starts. For a solo operator or an agency, that default position is exactly what makes it interesting as a service business.

## What it actually does

A workflow is a YAML file in your repo. GitHub runs it on a hosted machine when things happen: a push, a pull request, a new tag, a nightly cron. Typical jobs: run the test suite, build the Docker image, push to staging, notify Slack, deploy to production after a human clicks approve in an Environment gate. The Marketplace has 20,000+ prebuilt actions, so most of the plumbing - checkout, caching, cloud deploys - is copy-paste rather than shell scripting.

The AI part is no longer a press release. Copilot coding agent can be assigned a failing CI job and will come back with a fix PR that has to pass the same pipeline you wrote (our take on the broader tool lives at [GitHub Copilot](/tools/github-copilot/)). Copilot code review runs on Actions runners too. Neither replaces a DevOps engineer, but both shave real time off the fix-the-build loop that eats junior developer mornings.

## Pricing: the part everyone gets wrong

The headline "free" is real but narrower than people assume. Verified against GitHub's official billing docs (October 2026):

| Plan | Included minutes/mo | Storage | Per-user price |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free | 2,000 (Linux) | 500 MB | $0 |
| Pro | 3,000 | 1 GB | $4 |
| Team | 3,000 | 2 GB | $4 |
| Enterprise Cloud | 50,000 | 50 GB | $21 |

Public repositories: standard runners are free and unlimited, full stop. Private repos burn metered minutes at rates that depend on the OS: Linux 2-core is $0.006/min, Windows $0.010/min, and macOS $0.062/min - and the multiplier bites twice, because a Windows minute costs 2x your allowance and a macOS minute costs 10x. A Flutter team doing iOS builds discovered their "free" plan was costing $200/month and blamed GitHub; the billing calculator would have told them in thirty seconds.

Two more invoice surprises worth naming. First, storage: artifacts and Packages share one quota, billed by the GB-hour, and deleting artifacts mid-cycle does not refund what already accrued. Second, larger runners (the 16-64 core machines) are always billed - no free quota applies, even on public repos. Set budgets and the 90% usage alerts before your first real workload, not after.

## The money angle: sell the pipelines, not the tool

GitHub will not pay you to promote Actions - there is no meaningful affiliate or reseller program, so forget the commission route that works for marketing tools like [Instantly](/tools/instantly-ai/) or [GoHighLevel](/tools/gohighlevel/). What you can sell is labor, and the market for it is wide because the tool's "it just works" reputation hides how messy most teams' actual setup is:

- **Migrations**: plenty of shops still run a crusty Jenkins box or deploy over FTP by hand. Moving them to Actions is a $1,000-5,000 one-time project with obvious before/after proof.
- **Retainers**: once you own someone's pipeline, you own their release risk. $1,000-5,000/month for maintenance, security updates and being on call when Friday's deploy breaks is an easy renewal.
- **Productized rescues**: "your CI takes 45 minutes and fails randomly" is one of the most common and most fixable problems in software. Flat-fee pipeline audits and fixes convert well because the pain is specific. Pairing the pipeline work with the observability stack in [our DevOps monitoring comparison](/articles/best-ai-devops-observability-tools-2026-datadog-vs-new-relic-vs-dynatrace-vs-splunk/) turns a one-off into a bigger engagement.
- **Free-tier clients**: because Actions is free on public repos and nearly free on small private ones, your cost stack is almost nothing - the quote is nearly pure margin.

The honest downside of this angle: you are selling expertise, not residual software income. There is no recurring cut from GitHub, so revenue stops when you stop.

## Where it falls short

Be clear-eyed before standardizing on it. Deeply nested YAML workflows become a language one person understands, and debugging only approximates locally (the act project helps but is not the real runner). There is real lock-in: workflows do not survive a move to GitLab or a self-hosted setup. CircleCI still out-caches it for heavy parallel test suites, and Jenkins still out-controls it for teams that genuinely need a build farm - we put all four head-to-head in [Best CI/CD Tools 2026: GitHub Actions vs GitLab vs CircleCI vs Jenkins](/articles/best-cicd-tools-2026-github-actions-vs-gitlab-vs-circleci-vs-jenkins/). And macOS pricing makes it a poor default for mobile-heavy teams; a used Mac mini as a self-hosted runner often pays for itself in a quarter.

## Who should pick it

If your code is on GitHub and your workloads are Linux, it is the boring right answer: free for public work, pennies for most private projects, and a hiring market full of people who already know the syntax. If you run macOS-heavy builds at volume, price the self-hosted route first. And if you are looking for an income angle rather than a tooling choice, the migration-and-retainer path above is one of the more durable service businesses in the AI-tools space precisely because every new GitHub org is a future customer.

## FAQ

### Is GitHub Actions really free?

For public repositories, yes - unlimited standard-runner minutes. Private repos get 2,000-3,000 Linux minutes a month depending on plan, with Windows minutes billed at 2x and macOS at 10x against that allowance. Self-hosted runners are always free of metered billing.

### Why did my Actions bill spike suddenly?

Usually a macOS or Windows job, an unbounded matrix, larger runners (never covered by quota), or artifact storage creep. Check the per-workflow usage report - it is almost always one recently merged workflow file.

### How does it compare to Jenkins or CircleCI?

Jenkins gives control but you own the server; CircleCI caches better for big test suites; Actions wins on ecosystem and proximity to the code. Details in our CI/CD comparison article below.

### Can I actually earn money with it?

As a service provider: migrations, DevOps retainers and pipeline rescues, at $1,000-5,000 per project or per month. As an affiliate: no - GitHub has no meaningful commission program for Actions.
